faq.a: Loss of antithrombin III, protein C, and protein S in urine creates a hypercoagulable state, and hypo‑albuminaemia raises plasma viscosity.
faq.q: Why is nephrotic syndrome the biggest risk factor for RVT?

faq.a: Spontaneous recanalisation occurs in a minority; however, untreated thrombus risks extension and renal loss, so anticoagulation is standard.
Only in rare cases of massive clot burden causing IVC obstruction or when anticoagulation is contraindicated; endovascular thrombectomy is not usually available in low‑resource settings.
faq.q: Is surgery ever needed for RVT?

exam: A 7‑year‑old with steroid‑resistant nephrotic syndrome develops sudden left flank pain and dark urine – what is your immediate diagnostic step and why? — Perform bedside renal Doppler; it can detect a venous thrombus quickly and guides anticoagulation.
How does the loss of antithrombin III in nephrotic syndrome predispose to RVT? — Urinary loss reduces natural anticoagulant activity, tipping the haemostatic balance toward clot formation.

A child with RVT is hypotensive and oliguric; what complication are you most concerned about and what management priority does it set? — Acute renal failure; prioritize fluid resuscitation and start anticoagulation while protecting renal perfusion.

Why is unfractionated heparin preferred over warfarin in the acute phase of RVT in a low‑resource hospital? — UFH can be stopped rapidly, requires only aPTT monitoring, and does not depend on INR stability which is often unavailable.

What feature on ultrasound helps differentiate RVT from acute pyelonephritis? — Absence of venous flow in the renal vein with a filling defect versus normal flow with renal parenchymal edema in pyelonephritis.

A patient with RVT also has a new deep‑vein thrombosis; what does this indicate about the underlying pathology and how does it affect your treatment plan? — Systemic hypercoagulability; extend anticoagulation duration and consider prophylaxis during future nephrotic relapses.
Explain why aggressive diuresis is contraindicated in acute RVT. — Diuresis can worsen intravascular volume depletion, reducing renal perfusion and worsening venous congestion.

What long‑term strategy reduces recurrence of RVT in children with recurrent nephrotic syndrome? — Maintain remission with appropriate immunosuppression and use prophylactic LMWH during high‑risk proteinuric periods.
ai.title: Renal Vein Thrombosis
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Renal vein thrombosis (RVT) is a clot in the renal vein causing hematuria, flank pain and renal dysfunction. It is most common in children with nephrotic syndrome or systemic hypercoagulable states, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Clinical triad: sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, and rising serum creatinine.
In nephrotic syndrome, look for a new rise in proteinuria or edema after a period of remission.
sections.p: RVT is the formation of a thrombus within the renal vein, obstructing outflow and leading to renal congestion, haematuria and impaired filtration. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion plus imaging or indirect signs when imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Does the renal vein show absent flow or a filling defect? Positive result confirms thrombus; negative does not rule out if operator skill is limited.
Shows a filling defect in the renal vein and perinephric stranding; definitive if visualised.
Rises >30 % from baseline suggests renal impairment from venous obstruction.
Red blood cell casts indicate glomerular bleeding; massive hematuria supports RVT.

b: Mild: <30 % rise in creatinine, unilateral thrombus, no hypertension.
Moderate: 30‑60 % rise, bilateral involvement or extension into IVC, new hypertension.
Severe: >60 % rise, renal failure requiring dialysis, or pulmonary embolism.
sections.p: Severity is graded by renal function loss and extent of thrombosis. No universal staging system exists, but clinicians use a pragmatic three‑tier model.

b: Nephrotic syndrome (especially steroid‑resistant, heavy proteinuria >2 g/day).
Severe dehydration from diarrhoea or malaria.
Infection‑related coagulopathy (e.g., severe bacterial sepsis, malaria).
Sickle cell disease with vaso‑occlusive crisis.
Systemic lupus erythematosus or other autoimmune vasculitis.
Herbal remedies containing unknown pro‑coagulant substances.
sections.p: RVT is usually secondary to a hypercoagulable state. In African paediatric practice, the following are most common.

b: Gross hematuria – pink to cola‑coloured urine.
Acute rise in blood pressure due to renal ischemia.
Edema worsening in a child already proteinuric.
Possible fever if secondary infection or sepsis.
sections.p: Children often present while in bed with sudden unilateral or bilateral flank pain, visible blood in urine and a rapid decline in urine output.
Prioritise bedside‑available tests; if advanced imaging is lacking, rely on indirect markers.

t.b: Is renal function falling? A rise >30 % signals clinically significant obstruction.
Is there blood (+3 or more) without infection? Supports renal bleeding.
Is the affected kidney enlarged with absent venous Doppler signal? Suggests thrombus.
Are there abnormalities indicating consumptive coagulopathy? Guides anticoagulation safety.

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable – monitor urine output and creatinine trend
t.b: A falling output with rising creatinine still points to obstruction; treat empirically.

b: Progressive renal failure requiring dialysis.
Extension into the inferior vena cava with risk of pulmonary embolism.
Severe hypertension refractory to three agents.
Concurrent deep‑vein thrombosis or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents irreversible kidney loss and life‑threatening emboli.

b: Low‑molecular‑weight heparin (LMWH) is first‑line where monitoring of anti‑Xa is possible; it has predictable kinetics and less need for lab checks than unfractionated heparin.
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) if rapid reversal may be needed (e.g., impending surgery) or if LMWH is unavailable.
Avoid warfarin in the acute phase because INR monitoring is often unreliable in low‑resource settings.
Correct dehydration aggressively with isotonic fluids; avoid volume overload.
Control hypertension with ACE inhibitors or calcium‑channel blockers; avoid NSAIDs which worsen renal perfusion.
If nephrotic syndrome is active, optimise steroid or calcineurin therapy; treat underlying infection promptly.
sections.p: Treat the underlying hypercoagulable cause, start anticoagulation when safe, and support renal function.

b: Repeat Doppler ultrasound at 4‑6 weeks to confirm recanalisation.
Serial creatinine and urine protein checks every 2 weeks for the first 3 months.
Maintain remission of nephrotic syndrome; use prophylactic LMWH during relapses if proteinuria >2 g/day.
Educate families on early signs of flank pain or hematuria.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring reduces recurrence and preserves renal function.

b: Acute pyelonephritis – usually febrile, positive urine culture, and tender costovertebral angle.
Renal infarction from arterial thrombosis – sudden severe pain, often with atrial fibrillation history, and CT shows wedge‑shaped defect.
Nephrolithiasis – colicky pain radiating to groin, visible stones on ultrasound.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic RVT share hematuria or flank pain.

b: Normal Doppler ultrasound early in the clot formation; repeat if suspicion persists.
Serum creatinine may stay within normal range if the contralateral kidney compensates; watch urine output.
Coagulation screen can be normal in isolated RVT; do not rule out hypercoagulability solely on PT/INR.
sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite serious disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension (>160/110 mmHg) unresponsive to two agents
Signs of pulmonary embolism (sudden dyspnoea, chest pain)
Altered mental status or oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) despite fluids
